findings.problemStatement: Undergraduate and graduate students (roughly ages 18-24, plus international students) must self-manage money for the first time on IRREGULAR income (part-time wages + lump-sum financial-aid refunds disbursed once or twice a semester) while lacking budgeting skills — and the result is measurable harm. Roughly 68% of students run out of money at least once a year (1 in 5 do so 8+ times), 59% have considered dropping out over money, and ~80% say financial stress hurts their mental health, with ~16% saying it directly harmed academic performance (Hope Center / Ellucian 2024). The cost of NOT solving is concrete and severe: dropout risk, degraded grades, chronic anxiety, and avoidance behavior (43-49% of Gen Z avoid even checking their balance, which compounds the problem). The core unmet need is not 'a tracker' but help converting a large, front-loaded, lumpy inflow into a steady spendable amount, staying aware of small recurring drains (subscriptions, shared costs), and reducing money anxiety — the emotional job, not just the arithmetic job.

problemSegments.segment: Aid-dependent students living on lump-sum disbursements
problemSegments.description: Students whose main cash source is a financial-aid refund paid as one/two lump sums per term. MDRC 'Aid Like A Paycheck' shows lump sums don't last the semester; biweekly-style pacing measurably helped students budget and cut work hours. Most distinctly student-specific pain — no incumbent budgets around aid-disbursement cadence.
problemSegments.frequency: acute 1-2x per term at disbursement, chronic budgeting pressure daily

problemSegments.segment: First-time money managers with no budgeting habit
problemSegments.description: Students managing their own finances for the first time. Incoming students average only ~2 of 6 basic financial-literacy questions correct; >40% lack adequate financial literacy; only ~23% can explain what they owe and why.

problemSegments.segment: Students sharing costs with roommates and friend groups
problemSegments.description: Rent, utilities, groceries, group trips split across people, plus social awkwardness chasing repayment. Splitwise (100M+ downloads) proves demand, but shared balances live siloed from personal budget.
Gen Z averages ~8+ subscriptions; 35% paid for unwanted subscription, 25% missed cancellation window, 22% incurred missed-payment/late fee.
Multi-currency budgeting, forex losses on remittances, expensive money transfers, no US credit history, hidden cultural/social spend. Distinct sub-segment mainstream US budget apps do not address.

underservedGaps: No mainstream budgeting app models financial-aid disbursement cadence — turning a lump-sum refund into a paced 'runway to end of term' allowance is student-native and unaddressed by YNAB, Rocket Money, Monarch, Copilot.
Personal budgeting and shared/split expenses live in separate apps (budget app + Splitwise); roommate/group balances invisible inside a student's own budget, so true spendable cash is never accurate.
Irregular, mixed income (variable part-time shifts + episodic aid) poorly handled by tools built around a steady monthly paycheck assumption.
Emotional/anxiety job unaddressed: 43-49% of Gen Z avoid checking balances, yet incumbents assume an engaged user who logs in.
International-student needs (multi-currency view, remittance/forex awareness, no-credit-history context) ignored by US-centric incumbents.
Habit formation / literacy scaffolding for genuine first-timers is thin — incumbents optimize for people who already know how to budget.
evidenceOfExistence: Hope Center national survey (Ellucian/PRNewswire 2024): 59% considered dropping out over finances; ~80% negative mental-health impact; ~16% academic harm.
Danahy 2024 (Journal of Consumer Affairs) + Inside Higher Ed: ~71% experienced financial trouble while enrolled; ~68% ran out of money at least once/year; 1 in 5 ran out 8+ times.
MDRC 'Aid Like A Paycheck': lump-sum aid doesn't last the semester; biweekly pacing measurably improved budgeting and reduced work hours.
NASFAA / Inside Higher Ed literacy surveys (100k+ incoming students): avg ~2/6 correct, >40% inadequate literacy, only ~23% can explain what they owe.
Splitwise 100M+ downloads, explicit mission to reduce stress/awkwardness money places on relationships — proven demand for shared-expense tracking.
Recurly / Savanta / UNiDAYS subscription surveys: Gen Z ~8+ subs, 35% unwanted, 25% missed cancellation, 22% late fees.
Discover / US Bank / Bank of America Better Money Habits 2024-2025: 43-49% of Gen Z avoid checking balances due to anxiety; ~65% negative emotions about finances.
MPOWER / VisaVerge / iefa: international students lose money to forex gaps, lack US credit history, face multi-currency budgeting.

gaps: Most cited stats are Gen-Z-wide or all-student, not narrowly scoped to a single differentiator segment.
Direct qualitative voice-of-student (r/college, r/personalfinance) not pulled verbatim this pass — recommend user-research-agent capture primary quotes.
One primary source (PRNewswire Hope Center release) returned HTTP 403; corroborated via Ellucian newsroom mirror.
No willingness-to-pay evidence for students specifically — severity established, payment intent not yet shown.
Splitwise download count is market-existence proxy, not evidence of student-specific dissatisfaction with existing split tools.
